questions.stem: What does building a SQL database project for a warehouse produce?

options.text: A .dacpac file describing the database schema
A full backup of the warehouse's data and schema
A CSV file of each table's rows plus a schema file
A Power BI report

questions.explanation: Building a SQL project validates its object definitions and produces a .dacpac, a package of the schema that deployment tools compare with a target and apply.

questions.stem: How does a SQL database project describe the database?

options.text: As an ordered list of ALTER and migration scripts that you must run one after another against each target warehouse
As a single connection string that points to a reference warehouse, whose live schema is read and copied again at every deployment
As a declarative set of object definitions, such as CREATE TABLE scripts, from which deployment works out the changes needed
As a copy of the data in each table, exported so deployment can reload the tables in the target

questions.explanation: A project holds the desired state of each object. Deployment compares it with the target and generates the changes, so you don't write migration scripts by hand.

questions.stem: What happens when you publish a SQL project's built .dacpac to a target warehouse?

options.text: The .dacpac's data is copied into every table, replacing the rows the target warehouse already holds
Nothing changes in the target until someone runs the generated ALTER scripts by hand afterwards
The difference between the .dacpac and the target is calculated, and only the changes needed are applied
The target warehouse is dropped and then recreated from scratch from the object definitions in the .dacpac

questions.explanation: Publishing calculates the difference between the source .dacpac and the target database and deploys the changes, so the target ends up matching the project.

questions.stem: Put the steps of bringing an existing warehouse under a database project and deploying a change in order.

options.text: Edit the object definitions in the project
Create a SQL project from the existing warehouse's schema
Publish the .dacpac to the target warehouse
Build the project into a .dacpac

questions.explanation: You start the project from the current schema, change it, build to check it and produce the package, and publish the package to the target.

questions.stem: You create a SQL database project for a Fabric warehouse in Visual Studio Code. Which target platform do you choose?

options.text: Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pool
SQL Server 2022
Synapse Data Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric
Azure SQL Database

questions.explanation: Warehouse projects use the Synapse Data Warehouse in Microsoft Fabric target platform, so the build validates against what a Fabric warehouse supports.

questions.stem: A developer removed a column from a table definition in the warehouse project. Deployment to production must stop if the change would drop a column that holds data. Which publish option do you set?

options.text: BlockOnPossibleDataLoss to False
Include permissions in project to Yes
DropObjectsNotInSource to True
BlockOnPossibleDataLoss to True

questions.explanation: BlockOnPossibleDataLoss prevents a deployment that risks losing data, such as dropping a column that contains data. DropObjectsNotInSource would do the opposite and remove objects.

questions.stem: Someone turned on DropObjectsNotInSource in the production publish profile. What is the risk?

options.text: Objects in the target warehouse that aren't in the project are dropped, with their data
Objects in the project that don't exist in the target are skipped instead of created
The target warehouse's permissions and role members are copied back into the project's scripts
The build no longer produces a .dacpac

questions.explanation: DropObjectsNotInSource removes target objects that the project doesn't define, which can delete important tables and data in production.

questions.stem: You are deploying a warehouse project to a target for the first time and want to see exactly what T-SQL would run before anything changes. What do you do?

options.text: Select Generate Script and review it
Commit the project to Git
Select Publish and roll back if needed
Run the project build twice

questions.explanation: Generate Script produces the T-SQL that would bring the target in line with the project without changing the target. Publish writes the changes.

questions.stem: Your team publishes the same warehouse project to dev, test and production with different options for each. How do you avoid re-entering the options every time?

options.text: Edit the .dacpac file's options before each deployment to each environment
Create a separate project for each environment with its own option values
Store the options as deployment rules
Save a publish profile (.publish.xml) for each environment and reuse it

questions.explanation: Publish options can be saved to a publish profile and reused, with different profiles for different environments.

questions.stem: Which two prerequisites does a developer need to build and publish a warehouse database project from Visual Studio Code? Each correct answer is part of the solution.

options.text: Contributor or higher permissions on the workspace that holds the warehouse
A deployment pipeline with three stages
A custom Spark pool in the workspace
The workspace connected to GitHub
The .NET SDK installed

questions.explanation: The .NET SDK builds and publishes the project, and the developer needs Contributor or higher access to the warehouse. Spark pools, deployment pipelines and Git aren't required.
